case_study_insert.main_stem: Cedar Grove Catering (CGC) is a cooperative in the hospitality and contract-catering sector, employing a workforce of 100. Founded in 2015 by Habiba Yusuf, it operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and produces 20,000 units a year, one unit being a catered meal sold at an average selling price of $90. CGC plans to invest $520,000 in a new central production kitchen and chilled-delivery vans, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year and a variable cost of $30 a unit. Food waste has reached 6.8% of meals prepared and client complaints have risen to 18 a month, up from 11 a month last year.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report, Q1 2025: CGC prepared 5,000 meals in the quarter with 18 written client complaints a month, up from 11 a month last year, and food waste of 6.8% of meals, up from 4.3%. Average delivery punctuality was 91% against a 98% target. A survey of 560 event organisers found 63% would pay $6 more for a low-waste menu and 58% choose caterers on sustainability. Of 100 staff, 29 kitchen hands have not completed on-the-job food-safety training; off-the-job hygiene courses at the technical college cost $390 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Cedar Grove Catering as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Hospitality Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.25% to 4.0%, increasing the cost of CGC's $320,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.4% from $13.92 to $14.95 an hour from April 2026, affecting kitchen and delivery staff. (3) Food input-cost inflation has reached 12.8%, corporate event spending grew 2.9% and general inflation is 6.2%.

questions.question_text: CGC plans to fund part of its new central kitchen with a $320,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for CGC of using the $200,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Applying the $200,000 retained profit means CGC pays no interest or instalments on that part of the $520,000 kitchen and van project, which protects its cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $300,000 a year and faces a base-rate rise to 4.0%. Every dollar of interest avoided can instead absorb the 12.8% food input-cost inflation or fund waste-reduction measures, protecting the $60 contribution earned on each of the 20,000 catered meals.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral, so the cooperative's existing assets are not exposed to repossession if the new kitchen fails to win enough contracts — relevant while food waste is 6.8% and complaints have risen to 18 a month. It also preserves member control: no lender can impose operating conditions on how Habiba Yusuf and the members run CGC. Using the $200,000 first reduces the $320,000 bank loan actually required, lowering CGC's fixed debt commitment at a time when delivery punctuality is only 91%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CGC's funding and kitchen investment.

questions.question_text: CGC is promoting its new low-waste menu. Consider trade magazine advertising, local radio advertising, and social media food influencers. Which should CGC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade magazine advertising: Specialist catering titles can reach event organisers and procurement managers with a detailed, credible message about the low-waste menu, supporting the 58% of surveyed organisers who choose caterers on sustainability. However, print lead times are long and response is hard to measure, and the readership includes many firms outside CGC's local delivery area, so part of the spend is wasted while the cooperative is funding a $520,000 kitchen with a $320,000 loan.

Local radio advertising: Local radio is relatively cheap and can reach nearby corporate clients quickly with a simple sustainability message, with flexible timing around lunch and event seasons. Its weakness is that audio cannot show the menu or the waste reduction, and it reaches few of the decision-makers who commission large events, so it is unlikely to generate the 20,000 meals needed to justify the new kitchen.

Social media food influencers: Food and sustainability influencers can show the low-waste menu visually to the 63% of 560 organisers who would pay $6 more and the 58% who select caterers on sustainability. Content is shareable, targeting is precise and engagement can be tracked, though results build gradually and depend on credible influencers who understand corporate catering.

Recommendation: CGC should choose social media food influencers, supported by a small trade-magazine presence for credibility. Influencers demonstrate the low-waste menu and reach the sustainability-minded organisers behind the $520,000 investment, at a cost controllable from the $200,000 retained profit. Local radio is rejected because it cannot display the menu and reaches too few corporate buyers; trade magazines alone are rejected as slow and unmeasurable while CGC services a $320,000 loan and $300,000 fixed costs. Influencer content can also be reused in proposals to clients.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to CGC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CGC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CGC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and trade magazines are rejected.

questions.question_text: CGC has 6.8% food waste and 18 client complaints a month. Explain two benefits for CGC of its democratic leadership style in tackling these issues.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives CGC's workforce of 100 a say in how meals are prepared and delivered, so kitchen hands and drivers can suggest practical ways to cut the 6.8% waste, such as better portion planning or accurate order forecasts. Because the people who prepare the meals help design the solution, the changes are more likely to work, protecting the $60 contribution on each of the 20,000 meals and supporting the $520,000 central kitchen.

Point 2: Consulting staff also helps reduce the 18 monthly complaints and the 91% punctuality rate: drivers and chefs know where deliveries run late and can propose route or packing improvements that management may overlook. Involvement raises morale and commitment among members of the cooperative, which matters when the minimum wage rises 7.4% to $14.95 and CGC needs productivity from its workforce to absorb higher costs. Democratic leadership therefore attacks both waste and complaints through front-line ideas while keeping members engaged with the expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CGC's waste, complaints and expansion.

questions.question_text: CGC must train 29 kitchen hands in food safety. Consider on-the-job training and off-the-job hygiene courses at the technical college. Which should CGC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching the 29 kitchen hands in CGC's own kitchen covers the exact food-safety routines that underpin its catered meals and the 6.8% waste problem, so learning is directly relevant and staff keep producing meals. It costs no course fees, protecting cash while the cooperative services a $320,000 loan, and supervisors can correct unsafe practice immediately. The drawback is that trainers are working chefs whose output suffers, and inconsistent instruction could leave the 18 complaints unresolved if standards vary between shifts.

Off-the-job training: The technical college hygiene course at $390 per person gives recognised, up-to-date certification for all 29 kitchen hands, costing 29 × $390 = $11,310 — modest beside the $520,000 kitchen investment and affordable from the $200,000 retained profit. It also brings an external standard that can reassure clients, 58% of whom choose caterers on sustainability. However, it removes staff from the kitchen for several days, cutting meal capacity, and generic content may need adapting to CGC's own processes before it fully addresses waste.

Decision: CGC should choose on-the-job training first, adding college certification during quieter periods. On-the-job training targets the real food-safety and waste issues in CGC's kitchen, costs nothing and keeps all 20,000 meals on schedule while complaints are being reduced. Full off-the-job training now is rejected because taking 29 of 100 staff out of the kitchen would cut capacity and risk delivery punctuality, which is already only 91%; the $11,310 course can be phased in later without that disruption. CGC should track the 18 monthly complaints and the 6.8% waste figure after training to check that the chosen approach is improving both service and food handling.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CGC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of CGC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, kitchen capacity and food-safety relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CGC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($90 − $30) = $300,000 ÷ $60 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 catered meals a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $90 − $30 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CGC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 5,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 20,000 meals: CGC has a margin of safety of 20,000 − 5,000 = 15,000 units, showing how many meal contracts it could lose before failing to cover $300,000 fixed costs, useful while complaints are rising.
2. Use contribution per unit of $60 to assess the $6 low-waste premium: it would lift contribution to $66, indicating the extra revenue available to service the $320,000 bank loan.
3. Set volume targets for the $520,000 central kitchen: roughly 8,667 extra meals at $60 contribution would generate $520,000, so managers can track contract wins against the investment.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $300,000 ÷ 20,000 + $30 = $45.00 a meal and labour productivity of 20,000 ÷ 100 = 200 meals per employee, a baseline for measuring the 12.8% food input inflation and the effect of 6.8% waste.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 15,000 meals; $6 low-waste pricing analysis; contract-volume targets for the $520,000 kitchen; and unit-cost benchmarking at $45.00 with labour productivity of 200 meals per employee.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CGC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CGC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.19 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.77 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $40,000 inventories + $75,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $145,000; 2025 current assets = $62,000 + $88,000 + $28,000 = $178,000. Coverage of short-term obligations 2024 = $145,000 ÷ $145,000 = 1.00; 2025 = $178,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.19. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($145,000 − $40,000) ÷ $145,000 = $105,000 ÷ $145,000 = 0.72; 2025 = ($178,000 − $62,000) ÷ $150,000 = $116,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.77.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved only modestly. Coverage of short-term obligations rose from 1.00 to 1.19 because current assets grew by $33,000 while current liabilities increased just $5,000 to $150,000. However, the stock-excluding measure improved only slightly, from 0.72 to 0.77, and remains well below 1.00, so CGC still relies on selling food inventories to meet its short-term debts. That is a concern while it services a $320,000 loan and plans a $520,000 kitchen. The apparent improvement depends heavily on inventories rising from $40,000 to $62,000 and receivables from $75,000 to $88,000, while cash actually fell from $30,000 to $28,000. If clients pay late or stock cannot be used, the stronger headline position could quickly weaken.

Conclusion: CGC's financial position has improved slightly, but only just. The 1.00 to 1.19 rise in the broad measure is the more favourable evidence; the small 0.72 to 0.77 move in the stock-excluding measure shows the gain is not based on liquid assets. CGC should convert inventories into cash and tighten credit control before committing further funds to the new kitchen.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, cash and receivables movements and a justified conclusion on the limited improvement in liquidity.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CGC of launching the low-waste menu backed by 63% of surveyed event organisers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The 63% of 560 organisers who would pay $6 more for a low-waste menu lets CGC raise contribution per meal from $60 towards $66 without extra volume, helping cover $300,000 fixed costs and the $320,000 loan. Combined with the 58% who choose caterers on sustainability, the menu strengthens CGC's reputation during the 6.8% waste problem and supports the $520,000 central kitchen by giving clients a clear reason to choose the cooperative.

Disadvantage: A low-waste menu may require more expensive ingredients or careful preparation, which could raise the $30 variable cost per meal and offset the $6 premium if only some clients pay it. The 63% is stated willingness to pay, not guaranteed orders, so revenue is uncertain. Introducing new recipes while 29 kitchen hands still lack food-safety training could add to the 18 complaints and risk the 91% punctuality rate, especially with food input inflation at 12.8% and a 7.4% wage rise squeezing margins.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CGC's survey, costs and waste.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.0%, the 7.4% minimum wage increase and the 12.8% rise in food input costs will affect CGC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.25% to 4.0%): If CGC's $320,000 bank loan follows the base rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $320,000 = $2,400 a year (0.0075 × $320,000). This is small against fixed costs of $300,000 and can be largely avoided by fixing the rate. Dearer credit could make future borrowing for the $520,000 kitchen more expensive, but the direct annual effect on CGC is limited.

Minimum wage increase (7.4%, to $14.95 an hour): Kitchen and delivery staff are hourly paid, so this rise increases the wage bill across the workforce of 100 and cannot be avoided. The insert provides no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the correct judgement is qualitative against the given 200 meals per employee and $60 contribution per meal. With waste at 6.8% and punctuality at 91%, productivity must be protected if the wage rise is to be absorbed without raising the $90 price.

Food input costs (12.8%): These apply to every one of the 20,000 catered meals. The insert does not decompose the $30 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated honestly: if the whole variable cost rose 12.8%, that adds 12.8% × $30 = $3.84 a meal, or about $76,800 a year (20,000 × $3.84). Even a narrower rise would reduce the $60 contribution needed to fund the $520,000 kitchen. The $6 low-waste premium recovers only part of this, so supplier negotiation and menu design matter.

Conclusion: The 12.8% rise in food input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 20,000 meals and directly erodes the $60 contribution underpinning the $520,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is small and hedgeable by fixing the loan rate, and the wage rise can be partly offset through productivity and the $6 premium. Food-cost inflation therefore requires the most urgent management action.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to CGC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CGC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of CGC with a well-justified judgement that food-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
